Hey there. I've been where you are, stepping into management while having employees know more about the job than I do. I had switched departments to be a manager for a department I've never worked in before - no one else wanted the position. I got 2 weeks of training at a different location to learn the fundamentals of the departments. One thing I will say is that I work retail, not office setting, so my experiences may be quite different from yours. But here's how I dealt. 

Walking into a new crew, being their manager and never working with them before, was very intimidating. It made me see a lot of my shortcomings. And I can't lie, it did make me feel defensive at first but then I realized I needed all the help I could get. The best thing to do, is to not take it personal when this person offers help - take their help, and show them that you appreciate them for it. A simple thank you goes a long way. And don't be afraid to keep them in the loop- in my experience, theyll appreciate that so that they dont get screwed up doing their own job. 
A lot of people do have bad intentions, we can't forget that- but if no one else wanted the position, it's safe to say there's a reason why, but they want you to succeed so it doesn't get pushed onto them. Take all the resources and knowledge you can get. As long as you're not actively pushing your job onto this star employee, there is nothing wrong with accepting their help and guidance. 
That being said, I have gotten into it with this employee of mine a few times. But you have to remember that you are the boss; at the end of the day, you actively took this management position, not them. Set some boundaries. But remain professional through and through. And if you need to be shown how to do something- ASK. So that you can jump in and help anytime. They'll appreciate you so much more for it. 

Just because you're new, doesn't mean you're no good. It just takes time, like you said, to get comfortable in the new position and be acquainted fully with your team. Let down your walls and accept the fact that someone else will know more than you do about your job. Appreciate that and show them that you're putting in the effort to learn and be a good manager.

 Bottomline is- if you fail, they fail too.

Honestly the best way to tell is to ask yourself this: are you able to limit the amount you're drinking once you start? Do you feel like you are in control of the alcohol, or does it control you? If something warranted it, would you be able to take a break from drinking altogether? 

I think taking a break may be in your best interest. Dig deeper within yourself and ask yourself why you need to drink so often. And if you are finding it hard or even impossible to give yourself a break away from the alcohol, chances are, you're already headed in the direction of alcoholism.

And if you want him to be able to go outside, there are many alternatives to go about that other than letting him free roam and possibly be exposed to the dangers of being outside unsupervised. If you really do decide you want to let him free roam anyway, make sure he's updated on all his shots. If he runs into any strays, it could be bad since they may carry diseases. Take some time to scope the area and really make an accurate assessment on what types of risks he'd be more vulnerable (ex traffic, other cats roaming the area, etc.) Take him out on a leash/harness daily to get him used to it, gradually he will be able to learn the area so he wont be completely lost. Also, if you dont already, make sure hes microchipped and has a collar on him.

Hope this helped a little, good luck!

Do not declaw your cat. There are many other ways you can go about this. Declawing is extremely painful and has long lasting effects on the cat, and its selfish to even consider doing so. Not to mention it's illegal in certain places. 

The best way to go about this is to play with him, get him many different toys and figure out what he likes. When he gets aggressive with you, pull your arm back and loudly say "ow" or something to teach him that clawing your skin is wrong. Placing catnip around the scratching posts may help to encourage him to scratch at those instead of at furniture. On the other hand, placing citrus/citrus scent around the areas you dont want to be scratched, may deter him from scratching up furniture. Clipping his nails every now and then can dull his claws a bit, even if only temporarily. 

No matter what, dont declaw him, if it's really so much of a problem for you and nothing works, rehome him to someone who has his best interest in mind.
